person.name: Joseph_Brant
person.summary: Joseph Brant, also known as Thayendanegea, was a Mohawk military leader and diplomat during the American Revolution. He led British-allied Mohawk and Loyalist forces in the New York frontier war. After the conflict, he helped establish a Six Nations community along Ontario's Grand River and represented its interests in Britain and the United States.

conclusion: Joseph Brant helped establish the Six Nations community on the Grand River after the American Revolution and continued to press British and United States officials on Haudenosaunee land interests. The Haldimand Proclamation remains central to Six Nations land claims concerning the Grand River tract.

events.title: Birth in Ohio Country
events.description: Joseph Brant was born during the Mohawk hunting season along the Cuyahoga River in the Ohio Country. Mohawk hunters traveled there from Kanienkeh, their homeland in present-day upstate New York. His parents, Peter and Margaret Tehonwaghkwangearahkwa, were Christian Mohawks. Brant belonged to the [[Wolf Clan|Mohawk Wolf Clan]] and received the name Thayendanegea, meaning “He Places Two Bets Together,” in the [[Haudenosaunee Confederacy|Haudenosaunee Confederacy]].

Wolf Clan.explanation: The Wolf Clan was one of the matrilineal clans of the Mohawk people. Clan membership passed through the mother and shaped social identity and belonging.

Haudenosaunee Confederacy.explanation: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy, also called the Iroquois Confederacy, is an alliance of Indigenous nations that included the Mohawks. Its social and political organization included clans headed by clan mothers and male leaders.

events.title: Settles at Canajoharie
events.description: On September 9, 1753, Joseph Brant’s mother Margaret married [[sachem|Mohawk sachem]] Brant Kanagaraduncka at Canajoharie on the Mohawk River. The family lived in a substantial colonial-style frame house. They attended the Church of England and maintained ties with Sir William Johnson, the British Superintendent of Indian Affairs.

images.caption: Mohawk River at Canajoharie, New York
images.creator: Andre Carrotflower

sachem.explanation: A sachem was a civil leader in a Native American community. Kanagaraduncka was a Mohawk leader of the Turtle clan.

events.title: Serves in Seven Years' War
events.description: Beginning in 1758, Joseph Brant served with Mohawk and other Haudenosaunee allies in British operations against French forces in northern North America. He accompanied James Abercrombie’s expedition to [[Fort Carillon|Fort Carillon]] and witnessed the British defeat there. He later took part in campaigns that captured Fort Niagara and Montreal. The British awarded Brant a silver medal for his service.

Fort Carillon.explanation: Fort Carillon was a French fort at the southern end of Lake Champlain, later renamed Fort Ticonderoga. British forces under James Abercrombie suffered a major defeat there in 1758.

events.background:
At Fort Carillon, the Mohawk contingent watched from a hill as French fire cut down the British infantry sent to storm the fort. Abercrombie had kept the Mohawk in a scouting role. They were thankful to avoid the heavy losses of the assault. The expedition also brought Brant into contact with Guy Johnson, John Butler, and Daniel Claus.

At Fort Niagara, Brant scouted for the British. He joined British soldiers, New York militiamen, and other Iroquois warriors in the forest ambush at La Belle-Famille. The French relief force was destroyed while marching toward the fort. The article identifies this encounter as possibly Brant's first combat.

Amherst's force left Fort Oswego on August 11, 1760, for Montreal. After Fort Lévis fell, Amherst kept Indigenous allies out of the captured fort because he feared for the French prisoners. Most of the Six Nations warriors departed after being denied a share of its plunder. Brant remained with the expedition through the capture of Montreal in September.

events.title: Studies at Wheelock's School
events.description: In 1761, Joseph Brant began studying at Eleazar Wheelock's Moor's Indian Charity School in Lebanon, Connecticut, with two other Mohawk students. He learned English, arithmetic, farming, classical subjects, and religious subjects under Wheelock's guidance. There he met Samuel Kirkland.

events.title: Works as Interpreter
events.description: The article does not document Joseph Brant working as an interpreter in 1764. It states that he began working as an interpreter for the British Indian Department from 1766 onward, using his knowledge of English and several Haudenosaunee languages.

events.title: Translates Christian Texts
events.description: In spring 1772, Joseph Brant moved to Fort Hunter, New York, to stay with the Reverend John Stuart. He served as Stuart’s interpreter and taught him Mohawk. They translated the Anglican catechism and the Gospel of Mark into Mohawk.

locations.name_historic: Fort Hunter, Province of New York
locations.name_modern: Fort Hunter, New York, United States

events.background:
Brant had practiced translation during his schooling at Moor’s Indian Charity School. His interest in Christian texts continued while he was grieving Peggie’s death from tuberculosis in early 1771. The Church of England gave him spiritual comfort, and he remained an Anglican for the rest of his life.

He also asked Stuart to marry him to Susanna, Peggie’s sister. Stuart refused. Haudenosaunee custom accepted a widower’s marriage to his deceased wife’s sister, who could take the place of the lost wife within the household.

events.title: Appeals in London
events.description: In November 1775, Joseph Brant traveled from Montreal to London with Guy Johnson as the American Revolution spread through New York. Brant met King George III and colonial secretary George Germain. He sought British support for the Haudenosaunee Confederacy and protection for its land rights in return for an alliance with the Crown.

events.title: Fights at Oriskany
events.description: On August 6, 1777, Joseph Brant led about 400 Mohawk and other Indigenous allies with British rangers in an ambush near Oriska, New York. Sir John Johnson commanded the force. They attacked Brigadier General Nicholas Herkimer’s Patriot militia and Oneida warriors as the column advanced to relieve Fort Stanwix. Oneida support for the Patriot column brought divisions within the Haudenosaunee Confederacy into open armed conflict.

locations.name_historic: Fort Stanwix, Province of New York

images.caption: Painting of the Battle of Oriskany
images.creator: Egbert Norman Clark

events.background:
British plans placed the siege of Fort Stanwix inside a larger drive on Albany. Barry St. Leger’s expedition was supposed to come down the Mohawk Valley while John Burgoyne advanced toward the Hudson Valley. St. Leger’s force reached the Oneida Carry and began besieging the Continental post on August 2.

Herkimer’s relief column had left Fort Dayton two days earlier. It included about 800 militia members and a company of 60 to 100 Oneida led by Han Yerry. The militia were largely Palatine German farmers with little training. Herkimer sent three couriers ahead with a plan for Colonel Peter Gansevoort to acknowledge them with three cannon shots and send a sortie from the fort. The couriers did not get through until late the next morning.

On the morning of the fight, Herkimer had heard no signal and wanted to wait. His captains charged that he favored the British because his brother served with St. Leger. The column then entered a marshy ravine where the road descended more than 50 feet to a narrow stream. Seneca leaders Sayenqueraghta and Cornplanter had chosen the ground. The Royal Yorkers waited behind a rise while Haudenosaunee fighters lay concealed.

The American column lost about 465 men killed, wounded, or captured. Herkimer received a mortal wound. A sortie from Fort Stanwix looted the British-allied camp during the fighting. The loss weakened the morale of St. Leger’s Indigenous allies and contributed to the siege being abandoned two weeks later. Haudenosaunee oral histories call the battlefield “A Place of Great Sadness.”

events.title: Raids German Flatts
events.description: In September 1778, Joseph Brant led Mohawk and Loyalist fighters in a raid on the German Flatts settlements in the Mohawk Valley. After local residents took refuge in defended forts, the attackers burned farms and other buildings in an effort to damage a district that supplied Patriot forces.

events.date_note: The marriage occurred during the winter of 1779-1780
events.title: Marries Catharine Croghan
events.description: During the winter of 1779–1780 at Niagara, Joseph Brant married Catharine Croghan, daughter of British Indian agent George Croghan. Catharine held the office of [[clan mother]] in her Mohawk community. She and other Mohawk families had sought refuge at the British post at Niagara during the American Revolutionary War.

clan mother.explanation: A clan mother was a senior woman in Haudenosaunee society. Clan mothers nominated hereditary male civil leaders and took part in political decisions.

events.title: Fights at Newtown
events.description: On August 29, 1779, Joseph Brant joined John Butler, Butler’s Rangers, and Haudenosaunee and Delaware warriors at Newtown along the Chemung River near present-day Elmira, New York. Brant and Butler proposed harassing Major General John Sullivan’s advancing American army. Seneca leaders Sayenqueraghta and Cornplanter chose an ambush position. Sullivan’s larger force forced Butler’s Rangers and their Indigenous allies to withdraw.

locations.name_modern: Chemung River, New York, United States

events.title: Resettles on Grand River
events.description: On October 25, 1784, Governor Frederick Haldimand issued a proclamation granting Mohawks and other Haudenosaunee allies a tract along the Grand River in present-day southwestern Ontario. Joseph Brant led many families from former settlements in New York to the new community. The American Revolution had displaced them, and the British government had acquired the land from the Mississaugas.

images.caption: Mohawk Village on the Grand River, 1793

events.background:
Brant had identified the Grand River valley by early 1783. In May 1784, John Butler negotiated a purchase of about 3,000,000 acres from the Mississaugas of the Credit for £1,180. The proclamation followed three days after the Treaty of Fort Stanwix. Its language treated the new territory as a refuge for people who had lost settlements in the United States or wished to leave them.

The document described a corridor six miles deep on each side of the river. It ran from Lake Erie toward the river’s headwaters. It promised that the settlers and their descendants would enjoy the land forever. The proclamation was issued at the Castle of St. Louis in Quebec.

Its boundaries and legal meaning became contested. The Crown later said its purchase from the Mississaugas did not reach the Grand River’s headwaters, which lay about 30 miles beyond the boundary it recognized. Officials also limited leasing and sales to transactions with the government. Brant argued that the people living there held freehold tenure and could lease or sell land. A Six Nations-requested survey began in 1791.

events.title: Returns to London
events.description: In 1785, Joseph Brant returned to London as a representative of the Grand River Haudenosaunee communities. He pressed British ministers for secure title to their Grand River lands and compensation for wartime losses, and met religious and political figures interested in Mohawk affairs.

events.title: Negotiates New York Claims
events.description: In 1797, Joseph Brant traveled to New York with Mohawk leader John Deseronto to negotiate Mohawk land claims in the former colony. They agreed to settle the claims in exchange for payment from New York State. The United States Congress never ratified the agreement.

events.title: Moves to Burlington Bay
events.description: Around 1802, Joseph Brant moved with his family from the Grand River settlement to Burlington Bay. He had received a 700-acre grant at Burlington Beach. The family settled in a mansion on the estate.

events.title: Death at Burlington Bay
events.description: After an illness, Joseph Brant died at his home on Burlington Bay in Upper Canada on November 24, 1807. He was 64 years old.
